The imperfect subjunctive

To imagine what isn't real, Italian needs one more tense. Good news: it's very regular.

parlareaveredormire
ioparlassiavessidormissi
tuparlassiavessidormissi
lui/leiparlasseavessedormisse
noiparlassimoavessimodormissimo
voiparlasteavestedormiste
loroparlasseroavesserodormissero

The irregular ones to know: essere (fossi, fossi, fosse, fossimo, foste, fossero), fare (facessi), dire (dicessi), stare (stessi), dare (dessi).

", "

Se + imperfect subjunctive, then the conditional

This is the sentence for dreams and advice: an unreal condition, then its consequence.

Se avessi tempo, viaggerei di più.If I had time, I would travel more.
Se fossi in te, prenderei il treno.If I were you, I would take the train.

The trap for English speakers: in English, \"if\" is followed by the simple past (if I had), so you're tempted to use an Italian past tense. Not here: no \"se avevo\" — Italian needs the subjunctive, se avessi. And never a conditional right after se: no \"se avrei\", just as English doesn't say \"if I would have time\".

Don't mix them up

A real or likely condition keeps the indicative: \"Se ho tempo, vengo\" (if I have time, I'll come).

The same tense follows magari to express a wish: \"Magari fosse vero!\" (if only it were true!).
